ai_sets.subject: Pharmacology
ai_sets.title: Antiarrhythmic Drugs
ai_sets.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

questions.stem: Which Vaughan Williams class primarily blocks fast sodium channels?
questions.explanation: Class I antiarrhythmics are sodium-channel blockers that slow conduction in fast-response tissue.

questions.stem: Which class prolongs repolarization mainly by blocking potassium channels?
questions.explanation: Class III drugs block potassium channels, prolonging repolarization and refractory period.

questions.stem: A stable patient has a regular narrow-complex SVT dependent on the AV node. Which drug is the lecture's rapid AV-node 'off switch'?
questions.explanation: Adenosine briefly blocks AV nodal conduction and is used for AV-node-dependent re-entrant SVT.

questions.stem: Why must adenosine be given as a rapid IV bolus?

options.A: It has a half-life of about 10 seconds
options.C: It is poorly absorbed from muscle

questions.explanation: Adenosine has an extremely short half-life of about 10 seconds, so rapid IV administration is required.

questions.stem: Which condition is a major contraindication to adenosine in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Adenosine may cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma.

questions.stem: A patient has an irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with no consistent P waves. Which strategy is appropriate for ventricular rate control?

options.A: Beta blocker or non-DHP calcium-channel blocker

questions.explanation: For atrial fibrillation, the lecture uses beta blockers or non-DHP calcium-channel blockers to slow AV nodal conduction for rate control.

questions.stem: A wide, regular tachycardia should be considered which rhythm until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes that a wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A patient with tachyarrhythmia is hypotensive and confused but still has a pulse. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: Hemodynamic instability with tachyarrhythmia and a pulse requires synchronized cardioversion before detailed drug selection.

questions.stem: Which drug is specifically highlighted for torsades de pointes?
questions.explanation: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarizations and is used for torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: Which class reduces sympathetic effects, automaticity, and AV nodal conduction?
questions.explanation: Class II beta blockers reduce sympathetic cardiac effects, decreasing automaticity and AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Verapamil and diltiazem belong to which Vaughan Williams class?
questions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are Class IV antiarrhythmics and slow AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Which Class I subgroup causes moderate sodium-channel block and increases action-potential duration?
questions.explanation: Class IA has moderate sodium-channel block and also prolongs action-potential duration.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is especially associated with procainamide in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Procainamide can cause a lupus-like syndrome, especially in slow acetylators.

questions.stem: A patient has very fast irregular wide-complex AF with WPW. Which AV-nodal blocker should be avoided?

options.D: None; AV nodal blockade is preferred

questions.explanation: In pre-excited AF, AV-nodal blockers such as adenosine can favor rapid accessory-pathway conduction and should be avoided.

questions.stem: What is the key electrophysiologic effect of Class IC drugs such as flecainide?

options.A: Strong slowing of conduction with little effect on AP duration
options.B: Marked shortening of AV nodal refractory period

questions.explanation: Class IC drugs strongly block sodium channels and markedly slow conduction with little effect on action-potential duration.

questions.stem: Which Vaughan Williams class consists primarily of sodium-channel blockers?
questions.explanation: Class I antiarrhythmics are sodium-channel blockers and are subdivided into IA, IB and IC.

questions.stem: Which class primarily reduces sympathetic effects, automaticity and AV nodal conduction?
questions.explanation: Class II drugs are beta blockers; they reduce sympathetic effects, automaticity and AV nodal conduction.

questions.stem: Which class primarily blocks potassium channels and prolongs repolarization and refractory period?
questions.explanation: Class III drugs block potassium channels and prolong repolarization/refractoriness.

questions.stem: Adenosine terminates many AV-node-dependent re-entry SVTs mainly by:

options.A: Producing a brief AV nodal block

questions.explanation: Adenosine activates A1 receptors, lowers cAMP, increases potassium conductance and produces a transient AV nodal block.

questions.stem: Which drug is particularly useful for ventricular arrhythmias in ischemic myocardium and is given intravenously because of extensive first-pass metabolism?
questions.explanation: Lidocaine is a Class IB drug that preferentially acts on abnormal/inactivated sodium channels in ischemic ventricular tissue and is used IV.

questions.stem: Which Class IC drug should be avoided after myocardial infarction or in significant structural heart disease because of proarrhythmic risk?
questions.explanation: Flecainide is a Class IC drug and is contraindicated after MI/structural disease because of proarrhythmic risk.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is particularly important with chronic amiodarone therapy?
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights pulmonary toxicity/fibrosis as a serious amiodarone adverse effect, along with thyroid, liver, skin and eye toxicity.

questions.stem: Combining a beta blocker with verapamil or diltiazem increases the risk of:
questions.explanation: Both suppress SA/AV nodal activity, so the combination can cause additive bradycardia and AV block.

questions.stem: Which treatment is specifically associated with torsades de pointes in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes magnesium sulfate for torsades de pointes, along with correction of electrolytes and removal of QT-prolonging causes.

questions.stem: A stable 24-year-old has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190/min. Vagal maneuvers fail. Which drug is the best next step from the lecture?
questions.explanation: For a stable regular narrow-complex AV-node-dependent SVT, adenosine is used after vagal maneuvers fail.

questions.stem: A patient with WPW develops a stable, very fast irregular wide-complex tachycardia. Which drug is appropriate?
questions.explanation: In stable pre-excited AF with WPW, the lecture recommends procainamide and warns against isolated AV-nodal blockers.

questions.stem: A patient with prior MI and ventricular scar needs rhythm maintenance for paroxysmal AF. Which drug should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Class IC agents such as flecainide should be avoided after MI or in significant structural disease.

questions.stem: A patient on chronic amiodarone develops progressive dry cough, dyspnea and diffuse interstitial infiltrates. What is the most likely adverse effect?
questions.explanation: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary pneumonitis/fibrosis, one of its most serious toxicities.

questions.stem: A patient with HFrEF (EF 30%) needs pharmacologic maintenance of sinus rhythm for AF. Which is a reasonable option from the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture notes amiodarone or dofetilide as rhythm-control options in HFrEF, while Class IC drugs and verapamil are inappropriate.

questions.stem: A patient has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with HR 32/min, hypotension and dizziness. What is the initial drug?
questions.explanation: The lecture's clinical case identifies atropine as the initial drug for symptomatic bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient is pulseless with ventricular fibrillation. What is the most important immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: For pulseless VT/VF, the lecture emphasizes defibrillation and CPR first; antiarrhythmic drugs are adjuncts.

questions.stem: A patient has polymorphic VT with prolonged-QT physiology and a twisting QRS pattern. Which drug should be given?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies torsades de pointes as a prolonged-QT polymorphic VT treated with magnesium sulfate.

questions.stem: A patient with hyperthyroidism has atrial fibrillation and marked adrenergic symptoms. Which drug is especially useful initially?
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights beta blockers, including propranolol, for arrhythmias driven by sympathetic activation and hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: A patient with tachyarrhythmia is hypotensive, confused and has acute heart failure but still has a pulse. What should be done before choosing an antiarrhythmic drug?
questions.explanation: The lecture's first clinical principle is to treat the unstable patient first: unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse requires synchronized cardioversion.

ai_sets.subject: Physiology
ai_sets.title: Normal ECG
ai_sets.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

questions.stem: Which cardiac property cannot be directly assessed from a surface ECG?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that ECG evaluates electrical properties but not force of contraction or ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A depolarization wave moving toward the positive exploring electrode produces:
questions.explanation: Depolarization moving toward the positive electrode gives a positive/upward ECG deflection.

questions.stem: A repolarization wave moving away from the positive electrode produces:
questions.explanation: For repolarization, movement away from the positive electrode produces a positive/upward deflection.

questions.stem: The P wave represents:
questions.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization.

questions.stem: The QRS complex represents:
questions.explanation: QRS is ventricular depolarization; atrial repolarization is usually hidden within it.

questions.stem: Why is atrial repolarization usually not visible on the ECG?

options.A: It occurs with ventricular depolarization and is masked by the larger QRS
options.D: It is identical to the T wave

questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization overlaps ventricular depolarization and is obscured by the larger QRS complex.

questions.stem: A PR interval longer than 0.20 s most directly suggests:
questions.explanation: The normal PR interval is about 0.12–0.20 s; prolongation indicates conduction delay/block.

questions.stem: A QRS duration of 0.16 s suggests:
questions.explanation: Normal QRS is under 0.12 s; widening suggests delayed ventricular conduction such as bundle branch block.

questions.stem: Which ECG interval includes both ventricular depolarization and repolarization?
questions.explanation: The QT interval spans ventricular depolarization through repolarization.

questions.stem: A prolonged QT interval increases the risk of:
questions.explanation: The lecture links prolonged QT to ventricular arrhythmias, particularly torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: At 25 mm/s, how many large ECG squares equal one second?
questions.explanation: At standard speed, five large horizontal squares equal one second.

questions.stem: A regular rhythm has 4 large squares between consecutive R waves. The approximate heart rate is:
questions.explanation: For regular rhythm, rate ≈ 300 divided by large squares between R waves: 300/4 = 75/min.

questions.stem: Which finding is required for normal sinus rhythm in this lecture?

options.A: Each P wave is followed by a QRS and each QRS is preceded by a P wave

questions.explanation: Normal sinus rhythm is regular, 60–100/min, with a P before every QRS and normal PR/QRS durations.

questions.stem: Which leads are used in the lecture's quick approach to estimating the electrical axis?
questions.explanation: Lead I and aVF view the heart near 0° and +90° and are used to estimate axis.

questions.stem: The normal electrical axis range given in the lecture is approximately:
questions.explanation: The lecture gives a normal axis from about −30° to +90°.

questions.stem: Which myocardial function cannot be evaluated directly by an ECG?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that ECG evaluates automaticity, conductivity and excitability, but not contractility or ejection fraction.

questions.stem: An ECG represents which of the following?

options.B: The summed electrical activity of many myocardial cells detected at the body surface

questions.explanation: An ECG is not a single action potential; it is the summed electrical activity of many myocardial cells as it spreads through the heart.

questions.stem: Which leads are the standard bipolar limb leads?
questions.explanation: Leads I, II and III are the standard bipolar limb leads.

questions.stem: A depolarization wave moving toward the positive exploring electrode produces which ECG deflection?
questions.explanation: Depolarization moving toward the positive electrode gives an upward/positive deflection.

questions.stem: A repolarization wave moving toward the positive exploring electrode produces which ECG deflection?
questions.explanation: Repolarization moving toward the positive electrode produces a negative/downward deflection.

questions.stem: What does the P wave represent?
questions.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization.

questions.stem: What does the QRS complex represent?
questions.explanation: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization.

questions.stem: What does the T wave represent?
questions.explanation: The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.

questions.stem: Why is atrial repolarization normally not visible on the ECG?

options.B: It occurs during ventricular depolarization and is masked by the larger QRS complex
options.D: It is recorded as the U wave

questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization occurs at the same time as ventricular depolarization and is masked by the much larger QRS complex.

questions.stem: The PR interval normally lasts approximately:
questions.explanation: The lecture gives a normal PR interval of 0.12–0.20 seconds.

questions.stem: A normal QRS complex should generally be:
questions.explanation: The lecture states that normal QRS duration is less than 0.12 seconds.

questions.stem: Which ECG interval includes both ventricular depolarization and ventricular repolarization?
questions.explanation: The QT interval represents ventricular depolarization plus repolarization.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the T wave is usually in the same general direction as the QRS complex?

options.A: Depolarization and repolarization travel in exactly the same direction with the same polarity
options.B: Repolarization travels in the opposite direction and has opposite polarity, producing the same net ECG direction
options.C: The T wave is generated by atrial repolarization
options.D: The T wave is always inverted

questions.explanation: The lecture explains that ventricular repolarization is opposite in direction to depolarization and also opposite in polarity; opposite plus opposite gives the same net direction.

questions.stem: For a regular rhythm, heart rate can be estimated by dividing 300 by:

options.A: The number of small squares in the P wave
options.B: The number of large squares between consecutive R waves
options.C: The number of P waves in 1 second
options.D: The number of QRS complexes in 1 minute of paper

questions.explanation: For a regular rhythm, the lecture uses the rule of 300: 300 divided by the number of large squares between R waves.

questions.stem: A regular ECG has 4 large squares between consecutive R waves. What is the approximate heart rate?
questions.explanation: Using the rule of 300: 300 ÷ 4 = 75 beats/min.

questions.stem: An ECG shows a PR interval of 0.24 seconds. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.B: Delayed AV conduction / first-degree AV block pattern

questions.explanation: The lecture states that a prolonged PR interval indicates conduction delay or block; the companion ECG lecture links a long PR interval to first-degree heart block.

questions.stem: An ECG shows a QRS duration of 0.16 seconds. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.B: Delayed ventricular conduction such as bundle branch block

questions.explanation: A QRS wider than 0.12 seconds suggests delayed ventricular conduction, such as bundle branch block.

questions.stem: A patient has an irregular rhythm. Which heart-rate method from the lecture is appropriate?

options.B: Count R waves in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10
options.C: Count P waves in one small square

questions.explanation: For irregular rhythms, the lecture recommends the six-second method: count R waves in 30 large squares and multiply by 10.

questions.stem: An ECG has ST-segment elevation. Which type of process does the lecture associate with this finding?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that ST elevation or depression can indicate myocardial ischemia/injury, and its companion lecture associates ST elevation with myocardial infarction.

ai_sets.subject: Physiology
ai_sets.title: Physiology of Vascular Endothelium

questions.stem: In healthy vessels, endothelial hemostatic balance is normally shifted toward:
questions.explanation: Healthy endothelium favors anticoagulant and profibrinolytic activity.

questions.stem: Which endothelial mediators both inhibit platelet aggregation and promote vasodilation?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin inhibit platelet aggregation and dilate vessels.

questions.stem: Thrombomodulin limits coagulation mainly by inhibiting which activated factors in this lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists thrombomodulin as inhibiting factors Va and VIIIa.

questions.stem: Heparan sulfate on healthy endothelium enhances the activity of:
questions.explanation: Heparan sulfate enhances antithrombin III, which inhibits thrombin and factor Xa.

questions.stem: Which endothelial product promotes fibrinolysis?
questions.explanation: tPA activates plasmin and promotes fibrin clot breakdown.

questions.stem: Damaged endothelium promotes platelet adhesion mainly by releasing:
questions.explanation: vWF promotes platelet adhesion to exposed collagen after endothelial injury.

questions.stem: Which mediator is a potent endothelial-derived vasoconstrictor?
questions.explanation: Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor that stimulates vascular smooth-muscle contraction.

questions.stem: Which capillary type has the greatest permeability?
questions.explanation: Sinusoidal/discontinuous capillaries, such as in liver, have very high permeability.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing diabetes develops endothelial dysfunction. Which change is expected?

options.B: Increased NO and decreased adhesion molecules

questions.explanation: Chronic endothelial dysfunction shifts toward vasoconstriction and inflammation with lower NO and higher endothelin-1.

questions.stem: Why does increased endothelial permeability promote atherosclerosis?

options.A: It allows LDL to enter the vessel wall and contributes to foam-cell/plaque formation

questions.explanation: The lecture links increased permeability to LDL entry into the wall, foam-cell formation, and plaque development.

questions.stem: Which adhesion molecules are increased in chronic endothelial activation?
questions.explanation: Activated endothelium increases VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 to recruit immune cells.

questions.stem: Which factor is listed as a cause of endothelial dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Smoking is one of several listed contributors to endothelial dysfunction.

questions.stem: Endothelial VEGF production is most directly related to:
questions.explanation: VEGF promotes formation of new blood vessels as part of endothelial angiogenic function.

questions.stem: During acute endothelial dysfunction, histamine and bradykinin contribute to swelling mainly by causing:
questions.explanation: Acute inflammatory mediators increase vascular permeability, allowing plasma leakage and swelling.

questions.stem: Statins are listed as a strategy for endothelial dysfunction because they:

options.A: Reduce atherosclerosis progression and improve endothelial function

questions.explanation: The lecture lists lipid-lowering therapy with statins as a strategy to improve endothelial function and reduce atherosclerosis progression.

questions.stem: Which endothelial product inhibits platelet activation and aggregation while also promoting vasodilatation?
questions.explanation: Healthy endothelium releases nitric oxide, which is both vasodilator and antiplatelet.

questions.stem: Thrombomodulin contributes to the anticoagulant function of healthy endothelium mainly by:

options.B: Binding thrombin and promoting activation of protein C

questions.explanation: Endothelial thrombomodulin binds thrombin and promotes protein C activation, supporting anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A patient develops endothelial injury with exposure of subendothelial collagen. What is the most immediate hemostatic consequence?
questions.explanation: Exposure of subendothelial collagen after endothelial injury promotes platelet adhesion and aggregation.

questions.stem: Which endothelial mediator is most strongly associated with vasoconstriction?
questions.explanation: Endothelin-1 is a major vasoconstrictor released by endothelium, especially in unhealthy/dysfunctional states.

questions.stem: Which pair consists mainly of endothelial vasodilator mediators?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin (PGI2) are important endothelial vasodilators.

questions.stem: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) released from endothelial cells mainly promotes:
questions.explanation: VEGF promotes angiogenesis and formation of new blood vessels.

questions.stem: Which endothelial substances inhibit angiogenesis according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies thrombospondin-1 and endostatin as anti-angiogenic endothelial factors.

questions.stem: Endothelial angiotensin-converting enzyme contributes to vascular regulation by converting:
questions.explanation: Endothelial ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, particularly in pulmonary endothelium.

questions.stem: During inflammation, increased endothelial expression of ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and selectins primarily promotes:
questions.explanation: Endothelial adhesion molecules regulate leukocyte attachment and recruitment during immune and inflammatory responses.

questions.stem: An unhealthy endothelium releases more endothelin-1. What is the expected effect on local blood flow?

options.D: Increased flow due to reduced peripheral resistance

questions.explanation: Endothelin-1 causes vasoconstriction, reducing local blood flow.

questions.stem: Which change best characterizes endothelial dysfunction?

options.B: Reduced vasodilatation with a prothrombotic and proinflammatory state
options.D: Increased fibrinolysis with reduced platelet activation

questions.explanation: Dysfunctional endothelium shows impaired vasodilatation, increased thrombosis/inflammation, and abnormal vascular wall proliferation.

questions.stem: Which condition listed in the lecture can cause endothelial dysfunction?
questions.explanation: High blood glucose/diabetes is one of the lecture's listed causes of endothelial dysfunction.

questions.stem: Atherosclerosis promotes endothelial dysfunction in the lecture mainly in association with:
questions.explanation: High blood cholesterol/atherosclerosis is listed as an important cause of endothelial dysfunction.

questions.stem: Healthy endothelium helps maintain blood fluidity through which combination?
questions.explanation: The lecture summarizes healthy endothelial maintenance of blood fluidity as antiplatelet + anticoagulant + fibrinolytic activity.

questions.stem: Which outcome is most consistent with prolonged endothelial dysfunction?

options.B: Improved vasomotor tone and reduced thrombosis
options.C: Atherosclerotic progression with increased risk of ischemic cardiovascular events
options.D: Persistent vasodilatation with increased blood flow

questions.explanation: Endothelial dysfunction promotes impaired vasomotor tone, thrombosis, inflammation and arterial wall proliferation, contributing to atherosclerosis and ischemic events.

questions.stem: A patient has an inflamed vascular bed with increased endothelial ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and selectin expression. Which process is most directly promoted by this change?
questions.explanation: Endothelial adhesion molecules regulate leukocyte attachment and recruitment during immune and inflammatory responses.

ai_sets.study_guide_objectives: 1. Explore the primary functions of vascular endothelial cells. 2. Discuss the endothelium's role in maintaining homeostasis, including the balance of coagulation and fibrinolysis. 3. Understand the role of endothelial cells in angiogenesis. 4. Discuss the role of nitric oxide (NO) in maintenance of vascular health. 5. Analyze pathophysiological changes associated with endothelial dysfunction. 6. Discuss factors that cause endothelial dysfunction. 7. Explore potential therapeutic strategies targeting endothelial dysfunction.

ai_sets.subject: Physiology
ai_sets.title: Cardiac Cycle
ai_sets.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

questions.stem: Which event marks the beginning of ventricular systole?
questions.explanation: Isovolumetric contraction begins ventricular systole.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric contraction, ventricular volume remains constant because:
questions.explanation: All valves are closed, so pressure rises without filling or ejection.

questions.stem: The aortic valve opens when:

options.B: Left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
options.D: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure

questions.explanation: Ejection begins when ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure.

questions.stem: Approximately what fraction of ventricular ejection occurs during rapid ejection in this lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that about 70% of ejected blood leaves during rapid ejection.

questions.stem: The second heart sound is caused by closure of the:
questions.explanation: S2 occurs with closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the start of ventricular diastole.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric relaxation, which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The ventricles relax while all valves are closed, so pressure falls at constant volume.

questions.stem: AV valves open when ventricular pressure:
questions.explanation: Atrial pressure exceeding ventricular pressure creates the gradient that opens the AV valves.

questions.stem: During ventricular filling, volume changes from:
questions.explanation: Filling increases ventricular volume from end-systolic toward end-diastolic volume.

questions.stem: Atrial systole contributes approximately:
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction contributes about 20–25% of ventricular filling.

questions.stem: A third heart sound is associated with:
questions.explanation: S3 occurs with rapid inflow into the ventricle and is normally more likely in children.

questions.stem: A fourth heart sound is produced during:
questions.explanation: S4 is ventricular wall vibration during atrial contraction and is associated with a stiff ventricle.

questions.stem: At a heart rate of 75/min, cardiac-cycle duration is approximately:
questions.explanation: Cardiac cycle duration = 60/HR; 60/75 = 0.8 seconds.

questions.stem: Which phase has neither filling nor ejection?
questions.explanation: During isovolumetric contraction all valves are closed, so there is neither filling nor ejection.

questions.stem: During rapid filling, approximately what proportion of filling occurs?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that 60–70% of ventricular filling occurs during rapid filling.

questions.stem: Why does aortic pressure fall while the aortic valve is closed?

options.A: Blood continues to leave the aorta toward the periphery
options.B: The ventricle ejects into the aorta
options.C: The AV valves force blood into the aorta

questions.explanation: With no new ventricular inflow, blood continues to run off into the peripheral circulation, lowering aortic pressure.

questions.stem: Which change occurs during ventricular ejection?
questions.explanation: Blood leaves the ventricle during ejection, so ventricular volume falls.

questions.stem: The second heart sound is produced by closure of the:
questions.explanation: S2 is associated with semilunar valve closure.

questions.stem: AV valves open at the end of isovolumetric relaxation when:

options.A: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure
options.B: Aortic pressure falls below ventricular pressure
options.C: Atrial pressure falls below ventricular pressure

questions.explanation: An atrioventricular pressure gradient opens the AV valves.

questions.stem: During rapid ventricular filling, ventricular volume changes from:
questions.explanation: Ventricular filling increases volume from end-systolic toward end-diastolic volume.

questions.stem: Atrial systole contributes approximately what proportion of ventricular filling in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction supplies about 20–25% of ventricular filling.

questions.stem: Which best defines end-diastolic volume?

options.A: Ventricular volume at the end of systole
options.C: Ventricular volume at the end of diastole

questions.explanation: EDV is the volume in the ventricle at the end of ventricular diastole.

questions.stem: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 130 mL and an end-systolic volume of 50 mL. What is the stroke volume?
questions.explanation: Stroke volume = EDV − ESV = 130 − 50 = 80 mL.

questions.stem: A ventricle has an EDV of 120 mL and an ESV of 48 mL. What is the approximate ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: SV = 120 − 48 = 72 mL; ejection fraction = 72/120 × 100 = 60%.

questions.stem: Why does aortic pressure decrease during ventricular filling?

options.B: Blood continues to leave the aorta toward the periphery while the aortic valve is closed
options.D: Atrial contraction pulls blood from the aorta

questions.explanation: With the aortic valve closed, no new ventricular blood enters the aorta while blood continues into the peripheral circulation.

questions.stem: During ventricular filling, the aortic valve is closed but aortic pressure continues to fall. Which mechanism best explains this decrease?

options.B: Blood continues to leave the aorta toward the periphery while the aortic valve is closed
options.D: Atrial contraction pulls blood from the aorta

questions.explanation: With the aortic valve closed, no new ventricular blood enters the aorta while blood continues into the peripheral circulation.

flashcard_decks.subject: Pharmacology
flashcard_decks.title: Antiarrhythmic Drugs

cards.front: What does Vaughan Williams Class I block?
cards.back: Fast Na+ channels; it slows conduction in fast-response tissue.

cards.front: How do IA, IB, and IC differ?
cards.back: IA: moderate Na+ block + ↑APD; IB: weak Na+ block + ↓APD; IC: strong conduction slowing with little APD change.

cards.front: What does Class II do?
cards.back: Beta blockade → ↓sympathetic effects, ↓automaticity, and ↓AV nodal conduction.

cards.front: What does Class III do?
cards.back: Blocks K+ channels → prolongs repolarization and refractory period; may prolong QT.

cards.front: What does Class IV do?
cards.back: Non-DHP Ca2+ blockade slows AV nodal conduction; examples: verapamil and diltiazem.

cards.front: When is adenosine useful?
cards.back: AV-node-dependent regular narrow-complex re-entrant SVT.

cards.front: Why is adenosine given rapidly IV?
cards.back: Its half-life is about 10 seconds.

cards.front: Major adenosine contraindications in this lecture?
cards.back: AV block and asthma; bronchospasm can occur.

cards.front: What is the first question in tachyarrhythmia?
cards.back: Is the patient hemodynamically stable or unstable?

cards.front: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse: treatment?
cards.back: Synchronized cardioversion.

cards.front: Wide-complex tachycardia should be considered what until proven otherwise?
cards.back: Ventricular tachycardia.

cards.front: Drug highlighted for torsades de pointes?
cards.back: Magnesium sulfate.

cards.front: Why avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF/WPW?
cards.back: The AV node acts as a brake; blocking it can favor rapid accessory-pathway conduction.

cards.front: Important procainamide adverse effects?
cards.back: QT prolongation/torsades, hypotension, negative inotropy, and SLE-like syndrome.

cards.front: Rate control options for AF emphasized in the lecture?
cards.back: Beta blocker or non-DHP calcium-channel blocker in an appropriate patient.

cards.front: Vaughan Williams Class I?
cards.back: Na⁺-channel blockers: IA, IB and IC.

cards.front: Vaughan Williams Class II?
cards.back: β-blockers; ↓ sympathetic effects, automaticity and AV nodal conduction.

cards.front: Vaughan Williams Class III?
cards.back: K⁺-channel blockers; prolong repolarization and refractory period.

cards.front: Vaughan Williams Class IV?
cards.back: Non-DHP Ca²⁺ blockers: verapamil and diltiazem.

cards.front: Adenosine: key mechanism and use?
cards.back: Transient AV nodal block; useful for AV-node-dependent regular narrow SVT.

cards.front: Why is lidocaine useful after acute MI?
cards.back: It preferentially blocks abnormal/inactivated Na⁺ channels in ischemic ventricular tissue.

cards.front: Class IC drugs and key contraindication?
cards.back: Flecainide/propafenone; avoid after MI or major structural heart disease.

cards.front: Major amiodarone toxicities?
cards.back: Pulmonary, thyroid, liver, skin and eye toxicity; also bradycardia/QT effects.

cards.front: Torsades treatment?
cards.back: IV magnesium sulfate; correct electrolytes and remove QT-prolonging causes.

cards.front: Stable regular narrow SVT after vagal maneuvers fail?
cards.back: Adenosine.

cards.front: Stable pre-excited AF in WPW?
cards.back: Procainamide; avoid isolated AV-nodal blockers.

cards.front: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse?
cards.back: Synchronized cardioversion.

cards.front: Pulseless VT/VF?
cards.back: Defibrillation + high-quality CPR first.

cards.front: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia initial drug?
cards.back: Atropine.

cards.front: Why is β-blocker + verapamil/diltiazem risky?
cards.back: Additive bradycardia, AV block and negative inotropy.

flashcard_decks.subject: Physiology
flashcard_decks.title: Normal ECG

cards.front: What does a surface ECG record?
cards.back: The summed electrical activity of many myocardial cells, not a single action potential.

cards.front: Which cardiac property cannot ECG directly assess?
cards.back: Contractility/force of contraction or ejection fraction.

cards.front: Depolarization moving toward a positive electrode gives what deflection?
cards.back: Positive/upward.

cards.front: Repolarization moving away from a positive electrode gives what deflection?
cards.back: Positive/upward.

cards.front: P wave?
cards.back: Atrial depolarization.

cards.front: QRS complex?
cards.back: Ventricular depolarization; atrial repolarization is usually hidden within it.

cards.front: T wave?
cards.back: Ventricular repolarization.

cards.front: Normal PR interval?
Normal QRS duration?
cards.back: Less than 0.12 s.

cards.front: What does the QT interval represent?
cards.back: Ventricular depolarization plus repolarization.

cards.front: Why is prolonged QT important?
cards.back: It increases risk of ventricular arrhythmias, especially torsades de pointes.

cards.front: At 25 mm/s, how much time is 5 large squares?
cards.back: 1 second.

cards.front: Regular-rhythm heart-rate shortcut?
cards.back: 300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves.

cards.front: Core features of sinus rhythm?
cards.back: Regular, 60–100/min, P before each QRS, each P followed by QRS, normal PR and QRS duration.

cards.front: Quick leads for axis estimation and normal range?
cards.back: Use I and aVF; normal axis is about −30° to +90°.

cards.front: What cardiac functions can ECG evaluate?
cards.back: Automaticity, conductivity and excitability — not contractility.

cards.front: Which leads are bipolar limb leads?
cards.back: I, II and III.

cards.front: Which leads are augmented unipolar limb leads?
cards.back: aVR, aVL and aVF.

cards.front: What are the unipolar chest leads?
Depolarization toward a positive electrode produces what deflection?
cards.back: Positive/upward.

cards.front: Repolarization toward a positive electrode produces what deflection?
cards.back: Negative/downward.

cards.front: Why is atrial repolarization usually hidden?
cards.back: It occurs during ventricular depolarization and is masked by the larger QRS complex.

cards.front: Regular-rhythm heart-rate rule?
cards.back: 300 ÷ number of large squares between consecutive R waves.

cards.front: Irregular-rhythm heart-rate method?
cards.back: Count R waves in 6 seconds (30 large squares) and multiply by 10.

cards.front: Core normal sinus-rhythm criteria?
cards.back: Regular, 60–100 bpm, P before every QRS, normal PR, normal QRS.

flashcard_decks.subject: Physiology
flashcard_decks.title: Physiology of Vascular Endothelium

cards.front: Healthy endothelium favors thrombosis or antithrombosis?
cards.back: Antithrombosis: anticoagulant and profibrinolytic activity predominates.

cards.front: NO + prostacyclin: shared effects?
cards.back: Vasodilation and inhibition of platelet aggregation.

cards.front: Thrombomodulin's anticoagulant effect?
cards.back: Inhibits activated factors Va and VIIIa in this lecture.

cards.front: Heparan sulfate's anticoagulant effect?
cards.back: Enhances antithrombin III → inhibits thrombin and factor Xa.

cards.front: tPA versus PAI-1?
cards.back: tPA promotes fibrinolysis via plasmin; PAI-1 inhibits fibrinolysis.

cards.front: What does damaged endothelium release to promote platelet adhesion?
cards.back: von Willebrand factor (vWF).

cards.front: Main endothelial vasoconstrictor emphasized?
cards.back: Endothelin-1.

cards.front: Capillary permeability order?
cards.back: Continuous < fenestrated < discontinuous/sinusoidal.

cards.front: How does endothelium regulate inflammation?
cards.back: It controls leukocyte adhesion/migration using molecules such as selectins, ICAMs, and VCAM-1.

cards.front: Endothelial role in angiogenesis?
cards.back: Produces growth factors such as VEGF to promote new-vessel formation.

cards.front: Chronic endothelial dysfunction: NO and endothelin-1 changes?
cards.back: ↓NO and ↑endothelin-1.

cards.front: How does endothelial dysfunction promote atherosclerosis?
cards.back: ↑permeability lets LDL enter the wall; inflammation and adhesion recruit cells, promoting foam cells/plaque.

cards.front: Major causes of endothelial dysfunction?
cards.back: Hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, obesity, hypertension, smoking, inactivity, inflammation, oxidative stress, and aging.

cards.front: Acute inflammatory endothelial dysfunction causes edema how?
cards.back: Inflammatory mediators increase vascular permeability, allowing plasma leakage.

cards.front: Therapeutic approaches listed for endothelial dysfunction?
cards.back: Improve NO, reduce oxidative stress/inflammation, lipid lowering (statins), EPC therapy, and targeted endothelial signaling.

cards.front: Name three major ways healthy endothelium keeps blood flowing freely.
cards.back: Antiplatelet + anticoagulant + fibrinolytic actions.

cards.front: What does endothelial thrombomodulin do?
cards.back: Binds thrombin and promotes activation of protein C, supporting anticoagulation.

cards.front: What is the role of protein S in endothelial anticoagulant activity?
cards.back: It acts as a cofactor for activated protein C.

cards.front: What is the effect of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1)?
cards.back: It inhibits fibrinolysis and therefore favors a prothrombotic state.

cards.front: What does von Willebrand factor released by unhealthy/injured endothelium promote?
cards.back: Platelet adhesion.

cards.front: What happens when subendothelial collagen is exposed after endothelial injury?
cards.back: Platelet adhesion and aggregation increase.

cards.front: Which two major endothelial mediators cause vasodilatation?
cards.back: Nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (PGI2).

cards.front: Which major endothelial mediator causes vasoconstriction?
cards.back: Endothelin-1 (ET-1).

cards.front: What is the main angiogenic factor highlighted in the lecture?
cards.back: VEGF - vascular endothelial growth factor.

cards.front: Which two factors inhibit angiogenesis in the lecture?
cards.back: Thrombospondin-1 and endostatin.

cards.front: What metabolic reaction does endothelial ACE perform?
cards.back: Converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, especially in pulmonary endothelium.

cards.front: Which circulating mediators can endothelial cells degrade/inactivate?
cards.back: Bradykinin, serotonin, norepinephrine and prostaglandins.

cards.front: How does healthy endothelium affect local blood flow?
cards.back: It releases vasodilators such as NO and PGI2, increasing blood flow.

cards.front: How does unhealthy endothelium affect local blood flow?
cards.back: It releases vasoconstrictors such as endothelin-1, decreasing blood flow.

cards.front: Which endothelial adhesion molecules regulate leukocyte recruitment?
cards.back: ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and selectins.

cards.front: How does endothelium maintain vascular permeability?
cards.back: Through tight junctions and adherens junctions that regulate movement between endothelial cells.

cards.front: Name major causes of endothelial dysfunction from the lecture.
cards.back: Diabetes/high glucose, high cholesterol/atherosclerosis, hypertension, oxidative stress, metabolic syndrome, septic shock and some autoimmune diseases.

cards.front: What are the major consequences of endothelial dysfunction?
cards.back: Impaired vasomotor tone, thrombosis, inflammation and arterial-wall proliferation -> atherosclerosis and ischemic cardiovascular events.

Discuss the endothelium's role in maintaining homeostasis, including the balance of coagulation and fibrinolysis. 3. Understand the role of endothelial cells in angiogenesis. 4. Discuss factors that cause endothelial dysfunction. 7. Explore potential therapeutic strategies targeting endothelial dysfunction.

flashcard_decks.subject: Physiology
flashcard_decks.title: Cardiac Cycle
flashcard_decks.eligibility_verified_against: Study Guide- Circulation and Breathing module- 2026-2027

cards.front: What is the cardiac cycle?
cards.back: Mechanical, electrical, and valvular events from the beginning of one heartbeat to the next.

cards.front: Cardiac-cycle duration formula?
cards.back: 60 ÷ heart rate; at 75/min it is about 0.8 s.

cards.front: Main phases of the cardiac cycle?
cards.back: Atrial systole → isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation → filling.

cards.front: Atrial systole contributes how much ventricular filling?
cards.back: About 20–25%.

cards.front: What causes S4?
cards.back: Ventricular wall vibration during atrial contraction; associated with a stiff ventricle.

cards.front: Isovolumetric contraction: valves, pressure, volume?
cards.back: All valves closed; ventricular pressure rises; volume stays constant.

cards.front: What causes S1?
cards.back: Closure of AV valves at the start of ventricular systole/isovolumetric contraction.

cards.front: What opens the semilunar valves?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure rising above aortic/pulmonary arterial pressure.

cards.front: Rapid versus reduced ejection?
cards.back: About 70% of ejection occurs rapidly, then about 30% during reduced ejection.

cards.front: Isovolumetric relaxation: valves, pressure, volume?
cards.back: All valves closed; ventricular pressure falls; volume remains constant.

cards.front: What causes S2?
cards.back: Closure of the semilunar valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole.

cards.front: What opens the AV valves?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure falling below atrial pressure.

cards.front: How much filling occurs during rapid filling?
cards.back: About 60–70%.

cards.front: What causes S3?
cards.back: Rapid inflow into the ventricles during rapid filling; it may be normal in children.

cards.front: Why does aortic pressure fall while the aortic valve is closed?
cards.back: Blood continues to run off from the aorta into the peripheral circulation while no new ventricular blood enters.

cards.front: What opens the AV valves after isovolumetric relaxation?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, creating an atrioventricular pressure gradient.

cards.front: How does ventricular volume change during filling?
cards.back: It rises from ESV toward EDV.

cards.front: What happens to aortic pressure during ventricular filling?
cards.back: It decreases as blood continues to leave the aorta toward the periphery while the aortic valve is closed.

cards.front: What causes S3 in this lecture?
cards.back: Ventricular wall vibration during rapid inflow of blood from atria to ventricles.

cards.front: What is atrial systole's contribution to ventricular filling?
cards.back: About 20–25%; it completes ventricular filling.

cards.front: What defines isovolumetric contraction?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure rises while volume remains constant because all valves are closed.

cards.front: What ends isovolumetric contraction?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic/pulmonary pressure and the semilunar valves open.

cards.front: How does ventricular volume change during ejection?
cards.back: It decreases as blood is ejected into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

cards.front: What happens to aortic pressure during ejection?
cards.back: It rises with ventricular pressure during rapid ejection, then begins to fall during reduced ejection.

cards.front: What defines isovolumetric relaxation?
cards.back: Ventricular pressure falls while volume remains constant because all valves are closed.

cards.front: Define EDV.
cards.back: Ventricular blood volume at the end of ventricular diastole.

cards.front: Define ESV.
cards.back: Ventricular blood volume at the end of ventricular systole.

cards.front: How is stroke volume calculated?
cards.back: SV = EDV − ESV.

cards.front: How is ejection fraction calculated?
cards.back: EF = (SV / EDV) × 100.
